chapter.name: Real Numbers
chapter.blurb: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, HCF and LCM by prime factorisation, and using Theorem 1.2 to prove that square roots of primes (and expressions built from them) are irrational.

scope_in.item: State the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic and express a composite number as a product of primes (powers of primes, factors in ascending order) using a factor tree or direct factorisation
Find the HCF and LCM of two or three positive integers by the prime factorisation method, using the smallest/greatest powers of the common and involved prime factors
Use HCF(a,b) x LCM(a,b) = a x b to find the LCM (or HCF) of two positive integers when the other is known, and recognise that this simple product relation does not hold for three positive integers
Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic to decide whether a number of a given form can end in a particular digit, and to explain why a given expression is composite
State Theorem 1.2 (if a prime p divides a squared, then p divides a, for a a positive integer) and use it as a step in an irrationality proof

Prove that square root of 2, square root of 3, square root of 5 and simple expressions built from them (such as 5 minus square root of 3, or 3 times square root of 2) are irrational, using proof by contradiction together with Theorem 1.2

scope_out.reason: The chapter's own introduction (p.1) names this as part of 'Section 1.2', but Section 1.2 as printed (pp.2-6) covers only the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic; Euclid's division algorithm does not appear anywhere in this chapter's 9 pages -- a leftover reference from the pre-rationalisation edition, confirmed by reading every page.

scope_out.item: Decimal expansion of a rational number p/q (terminating vs non-terminating repeating), decided from the prime factorisation of q
scope_out.reason: Also promised in the introduction (p.1: 'we apply this theorem to explore when exactly the decimal expansion ... is terminating') but never developed; the chapter ends at section 1.4 Summary (p.9) right after section 1.3 (irrational numbers), with no decimal-expansion section. Another rationalisation-era leftover in the intro text.

scope_out.item: HCF/LCM by the long-division method or by listing multiples
scope_out.reason: Only the prime factorisation method is shown in this chapter (pp.4-6); no other method for finding HCF/LCM is taught here.

scope_out.item: The general proof of Theorem 1.2 (that a prime p dividing a squared implies p divides a), reproduced in full
scope_out.reason: The book itself marks this proof '* Not from the examination point of view' (footnote, p.6, tied to the asterisk before 'Proof :'). The statement of Theorem 1.2 and its use in later proofs remain in scope; deriving it from scratch does not.

scope_out.item: Proof by contradiction as a general logical technique
scope_out.reason: The chapter uses this technique repeatedly (pp.6-9) but explicitly defers its general explanation to 'Appendix 1' (p.6), which is not part of this chapter.

scope_out.item: Classifying real numbers as rational/irrational from first principles, locating irrationals on the number line, non-terminating non-recurring decimal representations of irrationals
scope_out.reason: The chapter explicitly recalls this as done 'In Class IX' (pp.1, 6) and only restates the p/q definition of an irrational number (p.6) in passing; it is not retaught here.

scope_out.item: Computing a three-number HCF or LCM directly from the general formulas in 'A Note to the Reader' (p.9)
scope_out.reason: Given only as enrichment with no worked example in this chapter -- the note's own cross-reference '(see Example 8)' points to an example that does not exist among this chapter's 9 pages (the chapter's examples stop at Example 7), a dangling reference from rationalisation. Tested here only as the qualitative fact that the simple two-number product rule fails for three numbers, verified directly via Example 4 (p.5).

concepts.name: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
concepts.description: Every composite number can be written as a product of primes, and this prime factorisation is unique except for the order of the factors.
concepts.idea: Multiplying primes together in different combinations builds every composite number, and a factor tree lets you take a number apart to see exactly which primes, and how many of each, were used.
concepts.rule: Every composite number x can be written x = p1 x p2 x ... x pn with p1, p2, ..., pn prime and p1 <= p2 <= ... <= pn; combining repeated primes gives powers, and this factorisation is unique once the primes are written in ascending order.
concepts.example: 32760 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 x 7 x 13 = 2 cubed x 3 squared x 5 x 7 x 13.

concepts.name: HCF and LCM by the prime factorisation method
concepts.description: Finding the HCF and LCM of two or three positive integers from their prime factorisations, using the smallest and greatest powers of the common and involved prime factors.
concepts.idea: Once every number is broken into prime powers, the HCF only keeps what all the numbers share (the smallest power of each common prime), while the LCM keeps everything any of the numbers has (the greatest power of every prime that appears).
concepts.rule: HCF = product of the smallest power of each common prime factor. LCM = product of the greatest power of each prime factor that occurs in any of the numbers.
concepts.example: 6 = 2 x 3 and 20 = 2 squared x 5, so HCF(6, 20) = 2 and LCM(6, 20) = 2 squared x 3 x 5 = 60.

concepts.name: The HCF x LCM = product relation (and why three numbers differ)
concepts.description: For two positive integers a and b, HCF(a,b) times LCM(a,b) equals a times b; this exact relation does not carry over to three positive integers.
concepts.idea: Multiplying the two numbers together and multiplying HCF by LCM both end up combining the smallest and greatest powers of every prime involved -- for two numbers these always turn out to match, but with three numbers, factors can be shared between just two of them and the simple match breaks down.
concepts.rule: For any two positive integers a and b: HCF(a,b) x LCM(a,b) = a x b. This lets you find LCM from a known HCF (or HCF from a known LCM). For three positive integers p, q, r in general, HCF(p,q,r) x LCM(p,q,r) is NOT equal to p x q x r.
concepts.example: Given HCF(306, 657) = 9, LCM(306, 657) = (306 x 657) / 9 = 22338. But for 6, 72 and 120: HCF = 6, LCM = 360, so HCF x LCM = 2160, while 6 x 72 x 120 = 51840 -- the two are not equal.

concepts.description: Deciding whether a power of a given number can end in a particular digit, and explaining why certain expressions are composite, by examining their prime factors.
concepts.idea: A number's last digit being 0 is controlled by whether both 2 and 5 are among its prime factors, and a sum is composite whenever every term in it already shares a common factor greater than 1, because that shared factor can be pulled out to expose a proper factor of the whole sum.
concepts.rule: A positive integer ends in the digit 0 exactly when its prime factorisation contains both 2 and 5. If every term of a sum has a common factor k greater than 1, the sum itself is divisible by k and so is composite (as long as the sum is bigger than k).

questions.a: Assume, to the contrary, that 7 times square root of 5 is rational, so 7 times square root of 5 = a/b for coprime integers a, b (b not 0). Rearranging, square root of 5 = a/(7b). Since 7, a and b are integers, a/(7b) is rational, so square root of 5 would be rational. This contradicts square root of 5 being irrational (proved earlier in this chapter). So 7 times square root of 5 is irrational.

Rearranges to get square root of 5 = a/(7b), a ratio of integers

questions.q: In the proof that square root of 2 is irrational, explain what would go wrong with the proof if the initial assumption had NOT included that a and b are coprime (i.e. if square root of 2 = a/b were assumed with no restriction on common factors).
questions.a: Without the coprime assumption, showing that 2 divides both a and b would not by itself be a problem -- a and b could simply already share the factor 2 (or more), so there would be nothing to contradict. The coprime assumption is exactly what turns 'a and b share a factor of 2' into an impossible conclusion, which is what makes the contradiction work.

questions.q: Construct your own expression of the form (an integer) plus or minus (an integer) times square root of (a prime number), different from every example already used in this chapter for this style of proof (not involving 2, 3 or 5 combined with square root of 2 or square root of 3), and prove it is irrational using the same style of proof.
questions.a: Answers will vary. For example, 4 plus 3 times square root of 7 (using the prime 7): assume it is rational, equal to a/b for coprime integers a, b. Rearranging, square root of 7 = (a minus 4b) / (3b), a ratio of integers, so square root of 7 would be rational -- a contradiction, since square root of 7 is irrational by the same method used for square root of 2, square root of 3 and square root of 5. So 4 plus 3 times square root of 7 is irrational.
